item.content:encoded:
A bridge with towers informed by a hockey slapshot has opened to public traffic between the United States and Canada after more than seven years of construction, decades of planning and a contentious back-and-forth with the federal government.

Named after Canadian-born Detroit Red Wings hockey player Gordie Howe, the bridge stretches over the Detroit River between the city of Detroit and Windsor, Canada.

It is "the first new crossing between Ontario and Michigan in over 60 years", according to the organising body the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority (WDBA).

WDBA coordinated the project, while design was led by AECOM.

On either side, the project includes border inspection facilities for travellers, while a toll-free multi-use pedestrian path stretches its length.

In total, it encompasses six bridge lanes, 16 toll lanes and 60 Canada and US inspection lanes.

Upon its completion, its main span is "the longest of any cable-stayed bridge in North America" according to WDBA, and its 720-foot-tall (220-metre) towers are among the tallest structures in the region.

AECOM bridge architect Erik Behrens, who was one of the first to drive across the bridge during opening ceremonies on 27 July 2026, said the towers' curves were designed to recall the arc of Howe's hockey stick mid-slapshot.

"The bridge's aesthetic appeal lies in the extreme slenderness of its gently curving deck,” said Behrens. "Together with the stay cables, it creates an impression of gravity- defying lightness and transparency."

Along with spanning a major trade route between Michigan and Ontario, the project now includes the largest ports of entry along the Canada-US border, according to the team.

Read:

Finland's longest bridge reaches completion in Helsinki

This has made the project a complex and political saga over the years, following its initial planning stages that started in the 2000s.

Most recently, US president Donald Trump has been attempting to block its opening after demanding that Canada hand over additional ownership of the bridge to the US, detail in a Truth Social post. It's currently jointly owned between Canada and Michigan, although Canada agreed to front the cost for construction.

In an original 2012 crossing deal, the two bodies agreed toll fees would go to Canada once the debt had been recouped; however, amidst Trump's outburst and threat of imposing tariffs, the deal structure is being relitigated.

The drama also caused Canada to disinvite the US from the bridge's opening ceremonies on Friday, 24 July, causing further tension.

However, the WDBA remained committed to opening the bridge to traffic on Monday, and for now, it's in use.

Elsewhere around the world, Finland's longest bridge was completed in Helsinki and Italy's former head of motorways was sentenced to 12 years in prison over a bridge collapse in Genoa.

The photography is courtesy of the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority.

item.content:encoded:
Stadiums are becoming more distinctive with clubs and countries using them to attract attention. As part of our Future Stadium series, we look at why stadium design is becoming more icon-focused.

UK-based Heatherwick Studio had never designed a stadium before, so its recent win in the competition to design Birmingham City's stadium – along with its design, which will see the stadium encircled in 12 giant chimneys – surprised many.

"As someone who bid for the Birmingham City stadium, it's fair to say I didn't imagine it as a Victorian factory," ZHA director Jim Heverin told Dezeen in a piece for this series.

The Heatherwick Studio-designed stadium will undoubtedly be distinctive, and it represents a growing trend where the owners of the world's best-known sports teams demand an aesthetically striking, unique structure.

"That's why we were put on the shortlist," Heatherwick Studio partner Eliot Postma told Dezeen.

"They probably knew what they were going to get from a lot of the competitors, and we were a bit of an unknown quantity."

"I haven't seen all of the other designs in the competition, but I wouldn't be surprised if ours was the boldest in its explicit landmark nature."

Increasingly, major sports clubs are huge global brands. Building this brand, along with the commercial capabilities that go with it, is a major part of a club's focus.

"Most clubs nowadays see themselves more as a brand than just as a sports entity, which may have been the situation like in the 70s or 80s when the focus was really 'we gotta win' and 'we're gonna have the greatest team'," GMP Architekten director Martin Glass told Dezeen.

"Nowadays, it's much more multifaceted, so they have to become like lifestyle brands. They earn as much money selling T-shirts as they earn from TV rights."

Real Madrid "wanted to have a statement"

According to Glass, who recently led the €1 billion overhaul of Real Madrid's Estadio Santiago Bernabéu, this change in thinking is having a marked impact on stadium design. While fan experience is still a priority, the need to create an iconic, eye-catching structure is a key part of the brief.

"Real Madrid has a very, very clear vision about the development of their brand, the possibilities and their whole future outlook," he continued.

"For them, it was absolutely clear that they wanted to have a statement that visually reflects their own visions, and so that was, of course, also an important task for us."

UK studio Foster + Partners, which is currently designing stadiums for three of the world's biggest football clubs – a 100,000-seat venue for Manchester United and a joint stadium for AC Milan and Inter Milan to replace the iconic San Siro, echoed this thought.

"The club's aspiration is to have an iconic, never-seen-before, timeless, you know, classic," Foster + Partners senior partner Angus Campbell told Dezeen.

"There's a bit of me that misses the 60s, 70s, 80s stadia"

Historically, many stadiums developed ad hoc over time. This resulted in unique forms, often with stands of different heights and eras surrounding the pitch.

However, throughout the 1980s and 90s, more and more stadiums were developed and built all at once, resulting in cohesive, aesthetically similar bowls. While these stadiums gave all fans consistent, unobstructed views of the pitch, they sometimes lacked the character of older venues.

"There's a bit of me that misses the 60s, 70s, 80s stadia that evolved over time," said Heatherwick Studio's Postma.

"In old stadiums you'd get like the South Stand and Tilton Road End – they'd be built in different periods and would have different characters, so you wouldn't get this completely homogenous appearance," he continued.

"From around the 80s through to now, there's often an incredible internal environment that gets slickly skinned with this sort of contemporary architecture that all too often does feel like a bit generic."

"You can't just copy-paste anymore"

With contemporary stadiums, studios are aiming to retain the high-quality viewing experience, but also create an iconic silhouette without becoming farcical.

"I don't think people are striving for a gimmick, as such," said Populous senior principal Maria Knutsson-Hall. "The fan has more expectations, but the owners also have more expectations, so you know you can't just copy-paste anymore and be the same as others."

"The identity of the building needs to be much more about placemaking than just creating a home for that club."

Read:

File into the Future Stadium

According to Foster + Partners' Campbell, the key to creating an iconic stadium is going beyond wrapping the stadium in a bright or colourful facade and really pushing engineering to be part of the form.

"Many stadiums try to create a unique identity," he said. "But if you try and do it in cladding and materials only, does that have the gravitas to stand the test of time?"

GMP Architekten director Glass gave Wembley Stadium, designed by Foster + Partners and Populous, as an example where "structural necessity" led to the creation of an iconic structure.

"Good architecture should be able to marry the aesthetic quality and the visual iconisation of a building with the actual technical requirements."

"[At Wembley] on one hand, it's a giant arch that holds a bit of roof, some floodlights, but being quality architects, of course, they were able to combine the two features," he continued.

"This is also something that for us as GMP is very important to have – structural necessity solved in a creative way to give it an aesthetic quality."

"We're not designing a jacket that's just arbitrary"

Campbell explained that the innovation seen at Wembley was part of Foster + Partners' design ideology, which is currently being developed in its design of Manchester United's stadium.

"We're not designing a jacket that's just arbitrary," he said. "It comes from an expression of how the stadium is accessed, used and sits within the city."

"With Manchester United, the whole reason is obviously that it has elements of the club's identity in the trident form, but it [the stadium's planned tent-like canopy] also has a functional role of making the stadium bigger than a stadium – extending the envelope to embrace the precinct."

Even though Heatherwick Studio's design for Birmingham City appears at first viewing to be slightly gimmicky, Postma explained that the design also came from a series of "quite logical decisions".

He explained that the fans had already responded to the design and were adopting it into chants.

"The second game after we released the design, there was a new chant going around the stadium of 'we are the chimney boys' – so for us, that's sort of the dream."

"Backlash in using branding or naming rights"

The focus on brand identity is also having another impact, not on the design, but on the naming of stadiums.

As clubs focus more on building their own brand, Populous' Knutsson-Hall predicts that we may see fewer stadiums named after sponsors as clubs consider naming rights as part of a wider branding strategy.

"There's a lot of fatigue, and also a backlash against using branding or naming rights," she said.

"What you do see now, particularly here in the UK, you see Tottenham Hotspur Stadium not a branded name, Fulham Riverside not a branded name, because they have many brands underneath that umbrella," she continued.

"So, the key thing in placemaking is to create an umbrella destination."

While football clubs are utilising stadiums to enhance their brand reach, countries are also commissioning stadiums with the direct aim of drawing attention to their country.

Foster + Partners drew attention to how the stadiums that hosted the past two World Cups provide an insight into how thinking is changing. The 2026 final was hosted in the relatively unrecognisable MetLife Stadium, which opened in 2010, while in 2022 Lusail Stadium, which was built specifically as a symbol for Qatar, hosted the final.

"The World Cup final has just been held in a stadium that I didn't even know what it looked like while the tournament was happening – I had no idea," said Campbell.

"[Whereas] Lusail is an instantly recognisable image," he continued. "The tournament was four years ago and probably no one could tell you what the other stadiums look like – they've forgotten."

Read:

What will the future stadium look like?

Campbell explained that Lusail Stadium was designed not only to host games, but to be a recognisable icon for the tournament.

"Lusail was about creating an identity for a country and a tournament," he said. "Suddenly you've got an audience of three billion watching the World Cup, if you're lucky, over the 10 games, maybe a million people actually got to visit it," he continued.

"We set out to create an emblem for a country and something that could be seen on the TV cameras for the global audience and become something that was identifiable for Lusail as a contemporary city and for the country of Qatar."

This trend looks to be continuing in Saudi Arabia, where a whole host of distinctive-looking stadiums are being built ahead of the World Cup in 2034.

item.content:encoded:
Granite cloaks the sweeping form of Shenzhen Natural History Museum, completed in China by architecture studios 3XN, B+H Architects and Zhubo Design.

Now officially open in the Pingshan District, the 100,000-square-metre building was planned as a new cultural landmark for Shenzhen.

It is distinguished by its fluid form that rises from the ground, designed by 3XN, B+H Architects and Zhubo Design to evoke nearby rivers and hills.

"Nothing in nature is square," said 3XN founder Kim Herforth Nielsen.

"Nature is amorphous, dynamic, and always in formation. From the beginning, the ambition was to create not a building, but a piece of landscape that had always been there – shaped by local geology, water and time," he continued.

"That idea has been carried all the way from the competition stage to the museum that opens today, a place where the story of our planet is experienced as a physical journey through terrain, light and space."

The design team 3XN, B+H Architects and Zhubo Design won a competition to design Shenzhen Natural History Museum in 2020 for a site beside Yanzi Lake. It is the largest natural history museum in southern China.

The museum's sweeping form rises from the ground with a sloping roof and terraces, which allow direct access from ground level to invite "everyday use beyond the threshold of the galleries", the studios said.

Externally, the museum is wrapped in strips of granite with openings intended to appear as though they have been carved within it.

Inside, it is divided across five cone-shaped volumes, linked by cave-like passages and atriums.

The galleries are dedicated to exhibits on natural history, as well as the ecology of Shenzhen and its surrounding region.

Photos of the galleries are yet to be released, but these have been developed with Atelier Brückner and Museum Studio to be "immersive, media‑rich environments". There is also a range of specimens on display alongside large‑scale installations.

Read:

Mecanoo completes rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi

"Shenzhen Natural History Museum is designed to interpret the laws of natural evolution and present the geographies of Shenzhen in a global ecological perspective," said the museum director Nan Zhaoxu.

"It brings together collections and research that trace 4.6 billion years of Earth’s history, but it is the architecture that makes this story tangible," he continued.

"By turning the museum into a living educational landscape – from the roof park to the cone‑shaped galleries – it allows visitors from Shenzhen and around the world to experience science, nature and place as one continuous journey that is specific to its place."

Elsewhere in Shenzhen, Urbanus recently designed a colourful school modelled on Hakka walled houses while MAD created a trio of "cloud buildings" for the Tencent headquarters.

Another natural history museum recently featured on Dezeen is the white, rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, which Mecanoo completed on Saadiyat Island.

The photography is by Adam Mørk.

item.content:encoded:
The long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, designed by the late architect Frank Gehry, is set to open its doors in December.

In a statement released today, Abu Dhabi's department of culture and tourism said the museum will open on Saadiyat Island on 11 December 2026, officially becoming the largest of the four Guggenheim outposts.

It is currently under construction in the island's cultural district, for which Gehry also designed the recently revealed Dar al Funoon Abu Dhabi performing arts venue.

Photos reveal building's clashing forms

"Guggenheim Abu Dhabi will open its doors on 11 December 2026, further strengthening Abu Dhabi's position as a leading global capital for the arts," read the department's statement.

"Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is a museum of modern and contemporary art and will be a space for encounter and exchange, promoting a more connected and diverse global community through art."

Plans for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi were first revealed in 2006, with construction beginning in 2011. Works were then suspended for several years, before restarting in 2019.

The building will be distinguished by its giant clashing forms, revealed in a new set of photos released today. These will contain galleries of varying heights and styles.

Alongside these galleries will be a centre for art and technology, as well as children's facilities, archives, a library and a conservation laboratory.

Once open, Guggenheim Abu Dhabi will be operated by the Solomon R Guggenheim Foundation and Abu Dhabi's department of culture and tourism.

Gehry found project "truly thrilling"

In 2021, it was revealed that the museum was scheduled for completion in 2025. At the time, Gehry described the project as "truly thrilling".

"I hope that this building is embraced by the people of the UAE and that this work will endure as a landmark for the country for many years to come," he said.

Read:

Abu Dhabi reveals plans for Frank Gehry-designed performing arts venue

Guggenheim Abu Dhabi's completion will follow the recent openings of other landmark cultural institutions on the island, including Jean Nouvel's Louvre Abu Dhabi in 2017 and Zayed National Museum by Foster + Partners in December 2025.

At 42,000 square metres, it will overtake Gehry's Guggenheim Museum Bilbao in size.

Other landmark buildings by Gehry, who passed away in December, include Walt Disney Concert Hall and Luna Arles.

The photos are courtesy of Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.

item.content:encoded:
UNESCO has updated its World Heritage List with 13 modernist buildings in Finland designed by architects Aino, Elissa, and Alvar Aalto.

Collectively known as Aalto Works, the group of buildings is one of 25 sites added to this year's World Heritage List, which also included a collection of 10 significant modernist buildings in Tashkent.

The Aalto Works buildings were selected for their contributions to shaping modern architecture globally and their approach to designing for wellbeing.

Five of the buildings are located in Helsinki, including The Aalto House, which was completed by husband-and-wife duo Aino and Alvar Aalto in 1936.

Buildings by Alvar Aalto and Elissa Aalto, who married after Aino's death, are also among the Helsinki-based buildings on the World Heritage List, including the architects' office, Studio Aalto, which was completed in 1955.

Completing the buildings in Helsinki that are on the list are the National Pensions Institute KELA, House of Culture and Finlandia Hall.

The list of Aalto World Heritage buildings is completed by eight significant projects elsewhere in Finland: Sunila Pulp Mill residential area, Paimio Sanatorium, Säynätsalo Town Hall, Seinäjoki Civic Centre, Muuratsalo Experimental House, the Aalto campus at the University of Jyväskylä, Church of Three Crosses and Villa Mairea.

Read:

Aaltos' Paimio Sanatorium set to be turned into "future-oriented" hotel by Snøhetta

"The Aalto Works series is unique from both a national and an international perspective," said Alvar Aalto Foundation CEO Tommi Lindh. "Until this designation, Finland had no sites of modern architecture on the UNESCO World Heritage List."

"These sites demonstrate the universal value of the Aaltos' human-centred approach to architecture and design, which brought together functionality, beauty and a deep understanding of people's everyday lives," he continued.

"Their inscription recognises the Aaltos' lasting influence on modern architecture worldwide and the enduring importance of creating environments that support human wellbeing, community and cultural identity across generations."

The Aalto Works was one of 25 new entries to the UNESCO World Heritage List this year, which encompasses human-built cultural locations and natural sites.

Also added to the list was the modernist architecture of Tashkent, Uzbekistan, represented by 10 buildings constructed between the 1960s and early 1990s.

Featuring museums, exhibition halls, hotels, residential developments and science facilities, the buildings demonstrate Tashkent's unique style of modernism, which was influenced by large-scale reconstruction efforts following the 1966 earthquake.

Other modernist buildings that made the UNESCO World Heritage List include the modernist city centre of Gdynia, Poland, and Berlin's Waldsiedlung Zehlendorf housing estate.

Several UNESCO-listed buildings have been damaged this year in ongoing wars. Tehran's 400-year-old Golestan Palace sustained damage following a nearby US-Israeli airstrike, the 17th-century Bernardine Monastery in Lviv was damaged by nearby Russian drone strikes and Kyiv's Dormition Cathedral was set alight during a Russian attack.

The photography is by Tuomas Uusheimo and Helsinki Partners unless stated.

item.content:encoded:
If the Glasgow School of Art cannot afford to rebuild the twice-destroyed Mackintosh Building it should transfer ownership to a trust that would enable a faithful restoration, writes Rory Olcayto.

For a brief moment, before the second fire in 2018, Glasgow School of Art's Mackintosh Building was reborn. Johnny Rodger captured it beautifully in his book Glasgow Cool of Art, recalling how the faithfully reconstructed library (pictured) offered not a replica, but a renewal – a building, and a city, recovering their spirit through the knowledge, care and craftsmanship of many hands and minds.

Despite the school's recent declaration that it alone cannot afford a faithful reinstatement, we must return to that moment, and complete it.

This is one of the defining achievements of Scottish culture

Any future for the Mack must begin with an understanding of what has been lost. It should be obvious that preserving only the surviving shell while replacing the interior with a new building – a scenario the school says it is prepared to explore, and which many fear is now its preferred option – would fundamentally misunderstand Charles Rennie Mackintosh's achievement: a synthesis of space, light, structure, material and detail, rooted in Glasgow yet reaching far beyond it.

Comparisons with Notre-Dame or the Sagrada Família are understandable but ultimately misleading. Notre-Dame is a state-owned medieval cathedral and the symbolic heart of France; Gaudí's cathedral in Barcelona is a century-long collective endeavour sustained over generations.

The Mackintosh Building is something different: Glasgow's secular church, where the city's belief in creativity, learning and the transformative power of making is given architectural form. It was built on the conviction that art, craft and design could enrich not only manufactured objects, but the cultural life of the city itself.

Read:

Glasgow School of Art "cannot rebuild" Mackintosh Building

It is also the fullest expression of The Glasgow Style – the world of Mackintosh, sisters Margaret and Frances MacDonald and Herbert MacNair, collectively known as The Four – where architecture, art and craft became inseparable. A door handle, a chair, a stained-glass panel and an entire building could all embody the same artistic idea.

In this respect, the Mack ranks alongside the Book of Kells and the Lewis Chessmen as one of the greatest works of art ever produced in Scotland. It should be faithfully rebuilt not because other countries reconstruct their monuments, but because this is one of the defining achievements of Scottish culture.

Precisely because of that status, the Glasgow School of Art's statement deserves close scrutiny. The task ahead is clearly daunting, but after eight years of reflection its language is strikingly managerial, describing the Mackintosh Building as a "heritage anchor for a wider creative innovation cluster".

The statement offers no explanation of why the insurance settlement is insufficient to fund rebuilding

Regeneration may follow from faithful reconstruction, but it is the consequence, not the purpose. Great works of architecture are preserved because they embody a civilisation's cultural values, not because they are economically useful.

The architecture profession's response has been similarly flat. A joint RIAS/RIBA statement welcomed the announcement but offered little challenge to a strategy that steps back from faithful reinstatement. Some caution is perhaps understandable: the RIAS President is a partner at Reiach and Hall, the practice appointed to undertake key preparatory work on the project – an excellent choice nonetheless.

Meanwhile, Stephen Hodder, who speaks for the school's board in the press release, was RIBA president when the first fire broke out in 2014, describing it then as "an international tragedy" and the library as "one of the great interiors of the world". Today, his emphasis is on an "updated business case" and a "gateway project".

Read:

Investigation into Glasgow School of Art fire fails to find "definitive cause"

The Mack now requires something more than professional endorsement of process: it requires an independent national voice arguing unapologetically for faithful reconstruction.

Other aspects of the statement stand out. The school claims it lacks the expertise to rebuild the Mack, despite having demonstrated after the first fire, under the guidance of Page\Park, that the library – the most delicate part of the whole building – could indeed be recreated. It also states that the school now "thrives" without the Mackintosh Building – an odd sentiment in a document intended to rally support for its reconstruction, unless, of course, it actively wants to relinquish ownership.

There are omissions too. The statement offers no explanation of why the insurance settlement is insufficient to fund rebuilding, despite asking others to help bridge the gap. Questions surrounding the second fire and the disparity between compensation and reconstruction costs deserve a full public accounting.

The time has come to transfer full responsibility, including ownership, to a dedicated national trust

Nor does the published timeline mention the abandoned architecture competition in which John McAslan + Partners were first declared winners, Hawkins\Brown later emerged as the preferred bidder, and the procurement was ultimately abandoned amid a reported potential legal challenge.

Most troubling of all is the proposal to create "museum-standard interpretations" alongside retained fragments of the building. The implication is that the experience of the Mackintosh Building can somehow be substituted by an interpretation of it.

There is another way. Carmody Groarke's rescue of Mackintosh's Hill House demonstrated how bold contemporary architecture can protect and reveal a masterpiece without diminishing it. The same spirit of invention should guide the Mackintosh Building. Faithful reinstatement is not an exercise in nostalgia but a demonstration of what Scotland can achieve when conservation, craftsmanship and architectural imagination work together.

Read:

"Glasgow School of Art simply cannot be razed"

We should rebuild the Mackintosh Building without the Glasgow School of Art – it has clearly exhausted its mandate as steward. Stewardship carries responsibilities as well as privileges, and after two fires, years of delay, a failed procurement process, a protracted insurance dispute and a public admission that the school neither needs nor can itself deliver the Mack's faithful reinstatement, confidence has inevitably been eroded.

The Mackintosh Building has outgrown the capacity of the institution it was built for. The time has come to transfer full responsibility, including ownership, to a dedicated national trust. The Glasgow School of Art should remain closely involved in the Mack's future – though as its friend, not its custodian.

Rory Olcayto is an architecture writer, editor and critic. He was formerly editor of The Architects' Journal and chief executive of Open City, the organisation behind Open House London. He studied architecture at the University of Strathclyde and previously worked in practice in Glasgow, Liege and Istanbul, and as a designer in the video-games industry.

item.content:encoded:
Tashkent's key modernist buildings from the 1960s, 70s and 80s have been listed by UNESCO as World Heritage Sites. Here, we round up the 10 buildings in Uzbekistan's capital that are now protected.

The collection of 10 buildings was recognised following the multi-year Tashkent Modernism XX/XXI research and preservation project led by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation.

"This inscription brings a vital part of Uzbekistan's recent architectural history into the international account of twentieth-century heritage and the global modernist movement," said Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation chairperson Gayane Umerova.

"These buildings record how Tashkent imagined public life, collective identity and the future through architecture," she continued. "The UNESCO recognition also carries a long-term responsibility: to conserve these buildings with rigour, keep them part of the life of the city and pass their knowledge to future generations."

Read:

Preserving Tashkent's modernist architecture an act of "cultural diplomacy" says cultural foundation's head

As one of the most populated cities within the former Soviet Union and the largest in Central Asia, Tashkent contains numerous municipal, cultural and residential buildings from the era.

Ahead of the listing, a team led by Milan-based architecture studio Grace, academic Boris Chukhovich, the Politecnico di Milano and Laboratorio Permanente carried out extensive research into the city's modernist architecture.

Below, Grace co-founder Ekaterina Golovatyuk and Chukhovich explain the qualities of the 10 buildings that are now UNESCO-listed:

Panoramic Cinema by Vladimir Beryozin, 1964

One of Tashkent's most iconic buildings, this cinema hall occupies a block that has a form informed by a doric column. An adjacent long, transparent block previously contained the foyer and cafe, although this has now been blocked up.

"The Panoramic Cinema (Palace of Arts) is the first in Central Asia and one of the first in the USSR immersive halls for viewing panoramic and widescreen films," said Golovatyuk and Chukhovich.

"Its aesthetics, the original layout and the unique design make it unequivocally the main masterpiece of Tashkent modernism and the most famous work of Tashkent architecture of the 20th century."

Lenin Museum by Yevgeny Rozanov and Vsevolod Shestopalov, 1970

Built to mark the centennial of Vladimir Lenin's birth, this building was one of the earliest museums dedicated to the former Soviet leader. It acted as a prototype for the other 13 built across the Soviet Union.

"The Lenin Museum (Museum of History) is a building that played a key role for Tashkent, on the one hand proving the possibility of introducing reworked traditional elements into the modern architecture of Uzbekistan, and for the USSR on the other, becoming a model of a memorial museum, repeatedly reproduced in other Soviet republics," said Golovatyuk and Chukhovich.

"An important indicator of the significance of the museum was the fact that even ideological opponents of the use of historical architecture forms in modern buildings recognised the quality, the grace and the elegance of the building."

Central Exhibition Hall of the Academy of Arts, by Rafael Khayrutdinov and F Tursunov, 1974

One of the largest exhibition halls in Central Asia, the two-storey building was set on a civic podium in a small garden. It was designed to display sculpture and applied arts on the ground floor, with paintings in the galleries above.

The entire building is surrounded by an arched colonnade with an angled facade decorated with a geometric mosaic.

State Museum of Arts by Iskander Abdulov and Anatoly Nikiforov, 1974 

The venue for the Where in the World is Tashkent conference, the State Museum of Arts is the headquarters of the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation.

One of the first purpose-built modern-art museums in the Soviet Union, the building was originally clad in a series of abstract, square panels. In the 1990s, it was renovated with new facades added, and now the organisation is considering returning the building to its original state.

"The most abstract and hermetic work of Tashkent modernism, the Museum of Art remains a testament to the possibility of designing a building as a work of art, even in a standardised construction industry," said Golovatyuk and Chukhovich.

"It was the first modern-art museum designed in Central Asia and one of the first in the USSR. Inspired by the possibilities of new materials, the building also betrays the architects' desire to transform the museum into a temple with its metaphysical and transcendental qualities."

State Circus by Genrikh Aleksandrovich and Gennady Masyagin, 1976

With a UFO-like form, the State Circus was one of numerous built in major cities across the Soviet Union. However, unlike the majority that follow a set Moscow-approved design, the Tashkent circus has a unique, futuristic identity.

"The Tashkent circus is an example of a creative initiative of Tashkent architects who defended the right to create unique local architecture at a time when architects in other cities could only adapt typical Moscow projects," said Golovatyuk and Chukhovich.

"The custom design of the dome, the new concept of the spectator foyer, the strong connection of the design with the historical Khadra Square – all this makes the circus an object that appeared at the right time in the right place, marking the new birth of the old city."

Chorsu Market by Vladimir Azimov and Sabir Adylov, 1980

The city's largest farmers' market, this building has a decorative green dome that encloses a large indoor market where the structure's steel frame is on display.

"For a long time, historians believed that the inspiration for the creation of the Chorsu market was the work of the Moscow architect Andrey Kosinsky," said Golovatyuk and Chukhovich. "However, we managed to establish more unexpected origins of this daring project, embedded in the very heart of the medieval part of Tashkent."

"The process, which began in the Algerian city of Sidi Bel Abbas and ended with the construction of a huge dome in the old city of Chorsu, could be a clear illustration of the concept of 'cultural transfers', through which architectural models developed in one part of the world are transformed beyond recognition in others, acquiring features and cultural characteristics of the context that accepts them," they continued.

People's Friendship Palace by Yevgeny Rozanov, 1981

Designed by the same Moscow institute that created the Lenin Museum, this building was also one of several of the same typology that were built across the Soviet Union.

Its style is very representative of Brezhnev-era architecture and the building is wrapped in a facade informed by technology, with concrete representations of bolt heads.

"The Palace of Friendship of Peoples is unprecedented in size, composition, constructive system, palette of materials, the amount of monumental art," said Golovatyuk and Chukhovich. "If we had to prescribe its place in the history of Tashkent architecture, the Palace could be considered a modernist version of Shchusev's Navoi theater."

"The gigantic building, in which Moscow architects reflected their ideas about the traditional architecture of Uzbekistan, has survived to this day in almost unchanged form," they continued. "The Palace is unique not only in terms of its aesthetics, but also for the construction technologies applied."

Metro station Prospekt of Cosmonauts by Spartak Ziganshin, 1984

Built in 1984, as the name suggests, this station is dedicated to the Soviet Union's cosmonauts. Richly decorated with marble and decorative glass lighting, the station is flanked by reliefs dedicated to Soviet space pioneers created by artist Boris Klochkov.

"Tashkent's metro, operating since 1977, was the first in Central Asia. At the urban scale, it represented a very important step in the modernisation of the city and was seen as more than a transportation system," said Golovatyuk and Chukhovich. "It had not only strategic defensive but also ideological functions, as it had to testify to the country's history and identity by means of the architecture of the stations."

"A team of local architects supervised by S Sutyagin designed the Cosmonauts Avenue station, quite original for its high spatial quality, fine finishes and numerous works of monumental art, inspired by the heroic conquest of space," they continued.

Zhemchug by Ophelia Aidinova, 1985

Designed to recreate the traditional collective living environments of central Asian mahallas, this residential tower block contains a series of stacked, three-storey courtyards.

"The architect Ophelia Aydinova decided to oppose the cheap prefabricated concrete housing, manufactured at the factory and mounted on the construction site, [for] the even cheaper construction technique implying construction in situ," said Golovatyuk and Chukhovich.

"Though the new technology ended up not being as economical as announced, Tashkent earned a brutalist masterpiece, attracting architects from across the world," they continued. "The concept and the layout of Zhemchug – the Pearl – has no analogues in the world – its shape was generated by the social ties in traditional Uzbek one-story neighbourhoods (mahallas), which Aidinova decided to re-interpret by erecting a multi-storey building with collective hanging courtyards."

Heliocomplex Sun, 1987

Located on a hill around 45 kilometres from Tashkent, the Heliocomplex Sun is one of the largest sun furnaces in the world.

Built as one of the last major scientific projects developed by the Soviet Union, it has a futuristic form and, with 12,090 mirrors, can heat materials up to 3,000 degrees Celsius.

"From a technological point of view, there are two similar solar furnaces in the world: in the city of Odeillo in the French Pyrenees and the Parkent foothills near Tashkent," said Golovatyuk and Chukhovich. "The French building appeared first, but its Uzbek successor was more ambitious."

"While the complex at Odeillo is completely utilitarian, the solar complex at Parkent was inspired by futuristic structures and cosmic dreams," they continued. "Functioning to this day, the sun institute testifies not only to the universality of the principles of modernist architecture, but also to its ability to adapt to various landscapes of the planet."

The photography is by Alexey Narodizkiy unless otherwise stated.

item.content:encoded:
Spanish designer Isern Serra has used rounded corners and curved built-in furniture to create a "relaxed and welcoming atmosphere" inside Napoli on the Road, a pizza restaurant in London's Soho area.

The central London restaurant has a pared-back, architectural interior that was inspired by chef Michele Pascarella's Italian roots.

"The project draws inspiration from vernacular Mediterranean architecture, where buildings are shaped by climate, craftsmanship, and local materials rather than trends," Serra told Dezeen. "The Mediterranean is understood here as a place where architecture is deeply connected to everyday life."

"Spaces are informal yet carefully crafted, materials are honest and timeless, and interiors encourage people to slow down, gather, and share meals," he continued.

Serra wanted the total interior design – rather than individual details – to define Napoli on the Road's Soho branch, which comprises an 80-square-metre ground floor and 35-square-metre basement.

With this aim, he kept the material palette restrained, introducing wood and stone furniture, walls made from a metal frame finished with plasterboard and flooring that functions as a neutral background.

"One of the key elements is the continuous flooring, which runs uninterrupted throughout the restaurant," Serra said.

"By avoiding changes in material or level, the floor creates a seamless landscape that visually enlarges the space while reinforcing a feeling of calm and permanence. It provides a neutral canvas upon which the rest of the architecture unfolds."

The designer also wanted to avoid, as much as possible, the use of individual pieces of furniture and instead chose to integrate some functions into the walls themselves.

"Seating, shelving and display areas become part of the walls, giving the space a sculptural quality while reducing visual noise," Serra said.

"This approach references the simplicity of vernacular Mediterranean buildings, where architecture and furniture often become one."

The deliberately pared-back design, with bare walls and simple lighting, was designed to have a soft and tactile feel, creating an interior that Serra hoped would reflect natural light.

"Instead of relying on decorative elements, the atmosphere emerges from the relationship between light, materiality and proportion," he said.

"Together, these choices create an interior that feels timeless, comfortable and deeply connected to its cultural references."

Curved and rounded openings, archways and furniture can be found throughout Napoli on the Road, another nod to the Mediterranean where "arches, softened corners, niches, and curved transitions appear naturally as a result of traditional construction techniques," Serra explained.

His aim was to reinterpret these traditional architectural shapes in a more contemporary way, while also softening the space of the two-floor restaurant and creating a sense of calm.

Read:

Interior of FUBA bakery in Madrid explores "dialogue between the ancestral and futuristic"

"Rounded corners, curved built-in furniture, and soft transitions create a continuous spatial flow that guides movement naturally through the restaurant," Serra said.

"The absence of sharp edges also generates a more relaxed and welcoming atmosphere, making the environment feel less formal and more intimate."

However, Napoli on the Road also features playful details, such as the dark red hue of the downstairs dining room and events space, and industrial elements including a metal bar counter – though even this has rounded edges.

"The stainless steel counter introduces a contemporary layer that balances the softness of the surrounding architecture," Serra said.

"While the rest of the project is characterised by warm textures, continuous surfaces and sculptural forms, the metal element provides precision, clarity and a subtle industrial quality."

This juxtaposition between the different materials also helps to create a more layered interior design.

"The contrast between the smooth, reflective steel and the soft mineral finishes creates a rich material dialogue that brings depth to the interior," Serra concluded.

Other recent restaurants featured on Dezeen include an eatery in Thailand enclosed by breezy louvre walls and OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum in New York City.

The photography is by Adrianna Giakoumis.

item.content:encoded:
De Montfort University design graduate Safaa Fojdar has developed a prototype for a portable device that uses suction to remove wrinkles from garments on the go.

The cordless device, called Elide, features a vacuum-style nozzle attachment that funnels warm air onto the clothing, while gentle suction removes light creases at a skin-safe maximum temperature of 45 degrees Celsius.

A refillable spray bottle integrated into the cap allows users to lightly dampen the fabric with water before hand, helping to release creases.

Fojdar told Dezeen she came up with the idea for Elide because she couldn't find any products on the market that can be used to reduce visible creases from clothes while still wearing them.

"If you're going to a formal event or an interview and your shirt gets creased in the car or on the train, there's not really anything out there that's effective and doesn't damage your clothing," she pointed out.

Her solution is based on the Coandă effect, which describes the way that liquid tends to hug nearby surface curves rather than flying straight off.

In this context, the introduction of moisture combined with suction from the nozzle pulls the fabric taut, while the warm air dries the misted water to lock the fabric flat.

"I wanted to tackle on-body use as safely as possible," Fojdar explained. "The nozzle attachment and the use of suction make it comfortable and easy to use because you can hold the fabric in place while removing wrinkles."

Read:

Overstimulated design student creates satisfyingly minimal focus timer

Fojdar argues that this solution for on-body crease removal offers an alternative to existing products such as wrinkle-release sprays, which can leave residue on clothing and need to be refilled regularly.

While the cordless operation is suited to quick touch-ups throughout the day, deeper creases are best tackled by using the device as a compact iron, which involves adding a hot plate attachment and plugging it into a socket to deliver the power required to reach temperatures of up to 200 degrees Celsius.

The ironing module features self-locking hinges that allow the hot plate to be folded away for compact storage, or opened up to create a flat surface that ensures a crisp finish.

Fojdar presented a working, 3D-printed prototype of Elide as part of De Montfort University's display at the New Designers event in London, which showcases the best emerging design talent in the UK.

Other exhibitors included James Murphy, who showed a children's chair that unfolds into a playset, and Carrie Lee with her satisfyingly minimal focus timer.

item.content:encoded:
German architecture studio GMP Architekten is part of a team renovating the Olympic Stadium in Montreal. The work includes replacing a membrane roof that caused problems for decades with a steel deck to protect the structure from falling icicles.

GMP Architekten was approached in 2018 for the project after several iterations of the roof had failed since the structure was completed in the mid-1970s. It was designed as a site to host the Summer Olympics and designed by French architect Roger Taillibert.

The Olympic Stadium is the centrepiece of the wider Olympic Park development constructed for the 1976 Summer Games in Montreal. The development included a fan-shaped velodrome that was later converted into the Montreal Biodome.

GMP Architekten, Schlaich Bergermann & Partner, WSP Global and Transsolar are acting as a consortium to renovate the stadium's roof, while other architecture studios, such as Lemay, have also joined the project.

The stadium's roof was originally designed with a Kevlar membrane textile that could be retracted via 26 cables suspended from the huge concrete tower that hangs over the structure.

However, the complexity of the mechanism that retracts the roof meant the stadium was not fully ready in time for the 1976 Olympics.

Because of this complexity, along with costs, union strikes and more, the project was never fully realised, and the city has struggled to produce a functional, durable roof for – much to the chagrin of locals and the wider architecture community. Local politicians even considered demolishing it.

Read:

GMP Architekten set to "reinvent" roof of Roger Taillibert’s Olympic Stadium in Montreal

GMP Architekten director Martin Glass, who has worked on several lightweight roof constructions, told Dezeen that the stadium's "visionary" nature made the project difficult to construct at the time.

"The building was so visionary that it was somehow also overburdening the competence of the Canadian construction industry way back in the early 70s," said Glass.

The team is renovating the roof, replacing the permanent Kevlar membrane while maintaining the iconic tower element.

This involves replacing the former retractable roof with a steel cap lined with a ring of skylights and a new outer steel structural ring. The 26 cables are being used to suspend this inner structure.

The cables will suspend up to 90 per cent of the roof's load.

"When the original tower was constructed way back 50 years ago, it was actually built to hold very high loads, and there were a lot of surveys and checkings done in the last 10 years on the tower, so we know it's absolutely structurally sound," Glass told Dezeen. "Therefore, we're able to put the majority of the loads of the roof to the tower."

Glass told Dezeen that replacing the heavier outer concrete ring with a lighter ring of steel and aluminium made the suspension possible, as "taking out the old technical ring gave [them] a lot of weight reserve".

The team is currently around 35 per cent through the inner part of the roof, which is being built on the stadium's floor.

After its completion, "mega cranes" will push the piece upwards. The cables will then be connected, the gap between the outer ring and interior roof sealed by skylights.

"Once the roof is fully finalised on the floor, we will have these big mega cranes that will push the whole roof up to its correct height of around 50 to 60 metres," said Glass. "Then the last step will be that the gap between the inner roof and the outer roof will receive a big hollow ring of glass."

The final roof will be covered with a white steel deck, as opposed to the now-infamous membrane roof that covered the stadium.

The permanent membrane put in place in the 1980s was constantly damaged by icicles that formed on the cables during Montreal's frigid winters, falling and puncturing the soft textile.

The phenomenon and other inclement weather forced the stadium to close in the winters.

"The current roof had something like 20,000 penetrations already," said Glass. "At a certain point, it's a bit dangerous".

"That's the reason we're not going for a membrane roof, but for a steel deck which has a special installation of shock-absorbing top cladding materials in addition to the original steel deck – just to make sure that nothing can really penetrate the roof."

Read:

Montreal students convert Olympic Stadium roof into design objects

"That will allow the client to use the stadium all year long, because you can imagine as an operator, it's a financial disaster to have a stadium that you can't really fully operate in winter."

Glass expects the inner roof will be finalised by the end of this year. Other work, including modernisation of the interior, was announced by Quebec's tourism ministry on 17 July.

Other updates, including overhauling tourist attractions such as renovations to an original cable car that travels up and down the concrete tower and the refurbishment of a glass observation deck, were announced in 2020.

The final roof will have an illuminated underside, and Glass said the skylights will allow the stadium to receive natural light for the first time.

"Although membrane is theoretically a material that can be executed in a translucent way, the original interior was completely dark, and there was no connection to the outside because," said Glass. "For whatever reason, way back in the 80s and also later in the 90s when they redid the roof, they chose an opaque membrane material."

"With the glazed ring that we're adding to the project, we're going to be able to have natural daylight in the stadium. And actually, for the first time, you'll feel whether it's day or night, or whether the sun is shining or it's raining."

Overall, the team wants to remain as close to the original design as possible, out of admiration for the project's structural ingenuity and unique spaces, such as the "hall of trunks" – a room towards the top of the tower containing the cable connections.

"It's such a landmark, and at least from the European view of Canadian architecture, it's actually the most prominent building in Canada," he said.

"It gets crazier and crazier the deeper you look into it, because they must have had quite a lot of freedom way back in '76, when they were doing the original project. There are so many spaces in this stadium that we're still quite astonished to see what they were doing with it and the possibilities they had."

He also said the public's attachment to the existing project informed their choices.

"There are quite a lot of people that are very emotionally attached to the existing project and to the existing roof," said Glass.

"We did not want to do anything that really sticks out. This building is already so strong, with its organic quality and sculptural expressiveness. We understood that the new roof must actually try to step back a bit and not be another crazy attraction, but be something that supports the organic forms, the original shape and the original intention."

The photography is by Patrick Beaudry of Snape Photo unless otherwise stated.

item.content:encoded:
American studio Elizabeth Herrmann Architecture + Design has used burnt-cedar cladding to help the Milo House blend with the wooded terrain in rural Vermont.

Located in the town of Cornwall, the house was designed for a couple and their dog, Milo, who were relocating from Boston.

The verdant area offers orchards, woods and distant views of the Adirondack Mountains, all of which "shaped the project from the outset", said Elizabeth Herrmann Architecture + Design, a Vermont-based studio.

Set on a hillside, the house is composed of irregular, offset forms that were designed to "dissolve into the forest".

"The residence stands quietly among a dense stand of trees, its bark-like exterior receding into the forest while luminous interiors open toward distant Adirondack views," the team said.

Facades are clad in blackened Japanese cedar that was charred using yakisugi, a traditional Japanese method that is often referred to as shou sugi ban in English.

The method involves treating wood using intense flames to enhance its "durability, dimensional stability and resistance to rot and pests", said the team.

"Yakisugi aligned closely with the homeowners' goals for a low-maintenance, high-performance exterior while also reinforcing the home's bark-like aesthetic and connection to the surrounding landscape," the team said.

The wood was sourced from Nakamoto Forestry, a Japanese company founded in 1959.

The team used the company's gendai variation, which is brushed once after the burning process to soften the soot and reveal the wood's natural grain below the carbonised surface.

Read:

Cordero Pardee juxtaposes "old and new material cultures" for Vermont barn conversion

In contrast to the dark facades, the interior of the home is bright and airy. One finds "cathedral-like" rooms, earthy finishes and an abundance of natural light.

"Lofted ceilings are paired with a wood acoustical ceiling treatment to soften sound within the expansive gathering spaces," the team said.

The house also features more intimate rooms for remote work.

Beyond the main residence, the project included a detached sauna and a garden shed – both of which were clad using the same yakisuigi cladding to create "a cohesive architectural language across the property".

Other projects in Vermont include a tiny house for an artist by Elizabeth Herrmann that has a sloped roof and cut-out corners, and the conversion of a barn into a private studio and library that was designed by Cordero Pardee.

The photography is by Ryan Bent.

item.content:encoded:
Scale-shaped shingles cover the sweeping, canopy-like roof of Casa Mac, an annexe in Vietnam designed by local architecture studio CTA.

Serving as an annexe to the client's existing home in Phu My near Ho Chi Minh City, Casa Mac was conceived as a large, singular living space. It is open to the elements and flanked on either side by a vegetable garden and koi pool.

CTA, which stands for Creative Architects, sheltered this space with a gently curving, canopy-like roof, bisected at its centre by a long skylight through which light is filtered by a series of hanging, perforated metal screens.

"We wanted to draw nature into the living space as much as possible, while minimising or concealing typical residential elements like doors, roofs, and walls," co-founder Nguyen Thanh told Dezeen.

"This, combined with the vaulted arch, evokes the sensation of being inside a cave," she continued. "All daily human activities and elements of nature coexist harmoniously beneath a single, expansive canopy of shade."

Long walls of exposed brick flank either side of the space, with the only concession to partition walls and doors being made for a slim block containing a rest room and bathroom along the southern edge. This is accessed via tall, arched openings.

The large central area is divided into different zones by a series of green spaces, with planters incorporated into two wide runs of steps that connect the lower living, dining and kitchen area to a slightly elevated workspace and jacuzzi.

To the west, stone steps lead across the koi pond to a parking area, where narrow arched openings in the brick wall lead through to the main home.

Read:

Perforated brick wall fronts breezy home in Vietnam by Live Out Studio

"The space did not need to function like a conventional residential home – the room next to the WC is specifically a rest room, not a bedroom, designed as a temporary spot where friends can take a quick rest or sober up if they have had too much to drink," Thanh said.

"Two small pathways cut through the thick brick walls to connect this annex with the old house at the front and back, providing seamless transitions while keeping the daily activities of the two households distinct," she continued.

Materials were chosen to be "raw and rustic", with the exposed red brick walls being complemented with a ceiling of narrow timber planks. Above, the roof is topped by scale-shaped bitumen shingles.

Previous projects by CTA include a narrow home in Bien Hoa, for which the studio used folding doors and perforated screens to allow for the mediation of light and ventilation, and a house clad in reused scallop tiles.

item.content:encoded:
Japanese vending machine manufacturer SDRS has developed a human-sized, stainless-steel fridge to stave off heatstroke amid the increasingly sweltering summers brought on by climate change.

The Do Hiemon Box serves as a one-person cooling booth, with vents that blow out cool air at temperatures as low as five degrees Celsius – about the same temperature as the chiller compartment of a refrigerator.

Industrial equipment supplier Trusco Nakayama, which is selling the product, says it can help to stave off heat stroke in just 20 minutes while using half as much energy as an average portable air conditioner.

The company compares the insulated stainless steel box to a "human refrigerator", with an interior height of 1.75 metres (5.7 feet) and a narrow seat designed to fit a single person.

The cool air is expelled from vents at the top and back, with three different levels allowing users to adjust the temperature and airflow.

Set on casters and powered using a regular plug, the booth can be easily moved around to offer construction and factory workers, and people attending outdoor events, a moment of respite from the heat.

Read:

Can we quit our air-con addiction?

Trusco Nakayama said the product was designed to provide "full body cooling", unlike the fan jackets or "fan-jakketos" commonly used by outdoor labourers in Japan, as well as by staff of the NTT Pavilion at last year's Osaka Expo.

The news comes after a record number of people in Japan suffered from heat stroke last year, leading meteorologists in the country to invent a new term: kokushobi.

The word, meaning "cruel heat day", is used when temperatures reach 40 degrees Celsius or above.

Last week, Japan experienced an unprecedented five-day streak of kokushobis, leading to 453 people being hospitalised in Tokyo in a single day – the highest number since records began more than a decade ago. The heatwave has killed at least 14 people across the country.

Air conditioning is a controversial method for coping with the increasingly scorching temperatures brought on by climate change because it contributes to the very heat it hopes to alleviate – both immediately by venting waste heat, and in the long term by leaking heat-trapping refrigerant gases and contributing three per cent of all global greenhouse gas emissions.

All of the imagery is courtesy of Trusco Nakayama.

item.content:encoded:
An office campus in central Manchester, designed by infrastructure company AtkinsRéalis, is tipped to become the future home of No 10 North – the northern outpost of 10 Downing Street.

Named the Manchester Digital Campus (MDC), the building is being built on brownfield land in the vibrant suburb of Ancoats, which was once the heart of Manchester's cotton mill district.

It has been billed as the future home of No 10 North, under British prime minister Andy Burnham's plans to decentralise government power from Westminster. It will serve as an extension of the No 10 Downing Street office in London, which has been the base for British prime ministers since 1735.

Groundworks have now started on the building, with the main build and completion expected for 2028 and 2032, respectively.

MDC will accommodate 8,800 civil servants

MDC is designed by AtkinsRéalis to accommodate approximately 8,800 civil servants from numerous government departments.

It will comprise approximately 84,000 square metres of workspace across two buildings on the site of the former retail park.

Plans for the MDC predate No 10 North, with it originally proposed to support the government's digital and data strategy and increase the number of civil servants in technology and digital roles.

Few details about the design have been revealed, but the visuals suggest the two buildings will have blocky forms with a gridded exterior lined with windows.

The senior responsible owner for MDC, Philippa Harvey, said the building will have "exceptional tangible benefits for the government".

"MDC is not just a new building – it is a transformation of how government works, bringing together digitally focused departments at scale in a purpose-built environment, fully embedded in the community we serve," explained Harvey.

"The new campus will help to harness the North West's digital expertise and foster collaboration across departments and the wider digital sector in the region."

No 10 North "not a gimmick"

No 10 North is planned to become the second centre of government, helping shift decision-making closer to the north of England.

However, as the MDC is not expected to complete until 2032, on Friday, Burnham's team has temporarily moved into Heron House – an office building in central Manchester currently home to Government Communications Headquarters, which is an intelligence and security organisation.

In an address, Burnham stated plans for devolution and establishing No 10 North were "not a gimmick", reported the BBC.

Read:

Carmody Groarke completes "transformative yet discreet" overhaul of Manchester museum

"There'll be many voices out there, I can hear them all already, often London-based, but not exclusively. They like to say, 'Oh, this will just be the new levelling up, or another sort of short-lived gimmick', and they'll also say 'What's it going to cost?'," Burnham said.

"What does it cost for everybody to troop down to London every time there's a meeting when you need to make an argument about something?" he continued.

"What does that cost? So actually, isn't it better that we have a North Pole that balances the South Pole of our country, where power will always be concentrated?"

Other government buildings recently featured on Dezeen include Nordic Office of Architecture's "open yet secure" New Government Quarter in Oslo and Shalom Baranes's plans for the White House ballroom.

The render is courtesy of the Government Property Agency.

item.content:encoded:
British architecture studio RSHP has completed One Shanghai, an 186-metre mixed-use skyscraper in central Shanghai, China, informed by the city's historical laneway network.

Located on Shimen First Road in Jing'an District, adjacent to the  Zhang Garden retail quarter, the 38-storey skyscraper is comprised of three volumes that contain office, retail and public spaces.

According to RSHP, the scale of the 89,000-square-metre development was informed by the preserved laneway network in Zhang Garden, a historical Shanghai site featuring a cluster of over 100 year-old Shikumen-style villas that have been converted into a retail district.

"The office tower rises as three distinct vertical volumes that increase in length towards the north, responding to the expanding geometry of the site and the fine grain of the two-storey buildings below," the studio explained.

The two lowest levels of the tripartite skyscraper are defined by an integrated external shading system on the facade with a colour palette and texture designed to reference that of Zhang Garden.

RSHP lifted the main tower volume above the lower two levels to create a setback from Zhang Garden's roofscape and preserve the views of the neighbourhood at street level.

Sky gardens located at level 35 and 37 offer panoramic views of the Shanghai skyline, as well as the low-rise roofscape of Zhang Garden below.

Inside the tower, the floorplates are arranged around a central service core, ensuring two corner positions with plenty of natural lighting and views through double-height glazing for every tenant, while allowing for flexible subdivision.

The building's connection to three metro lines, together with the street-level retail occupancy, required a careful curation of circulation to create a smooth flow of traffic.

RSHP designed an elevated office lobby above the ground-level retail, to allow free pedestrian movement from every direction to access the retail services and create an open-plan public space that connects the surrounding streets.

Read:

RSHP unveils design for "open and welcoming" Shenzhen skyscraper

The studio also added a dedicated metro entrance that leads visitors directly into the retail area above.

Car arrivals are located on the southern edge of the site to ensure the north-facing front of the building is free of disruption.

"Rather than treating transport infrastructure, heritage, public realm and workplace as separate programmes, the design brings them together into a unified experience that feels like a natural extension of the city," RSHP director Richard Paul said.

"From its three articulated volumes that respond to the site's changing geometry to the elevated office lobby, every element of the design works together to reflect the grain of the surrounding historic streets while returning the ground plane to the city as generous public space," he continued.

"The result is a tower that balances a distinctive skyline presence with sensitivity to its historic surroundings, creating a harmonious transition between old and new, public and private, and the city below and the workplace above."

The project was recently named Best Building Winner and Best Office Building Winner at the inaugural Council for Vertical Urbanism China Awards.

Elsewhere in China, RSHP has designed an office skyscraper in Shenzhen, featuring glazed office wings extended from a central concrete tower as well as a vast convention centre in Zhengzhou, with 16 exhibition halls connected by a mile-long elevated walkway.

item.content:encoded:
German hardware specialist Franz Schneider Brakel has updated and relaunched a door handle designed 40 years ago by influential industrial designer Dieter Rams, replacing its plastic parts with an all-metal design to make it more durable.

Rams originally developed the FSB 1138 handle during a workshop held at the Franz Schneider Brakel (FSB) headquarters in East Westphalia in 1986.

Led by German designer Otl Aicher, the workshop invited international architects and designers including Mario Botta and Peter Eisenman to rethink the door handle as a point of interaction between the human body and architecture.

Rams' solution presented a clear and intuitive form, comprising a circular rose, an index-finger recess and a gently rounded lever.

The product's simple shapes and graphic contrast are consistent with the designer's "less but better" approach, which he applied most notably in his role as head of design at German electronics company Braun.

He also designed furniture for Vitsœ, including the iconic 606 Universal Shelving System and the 620 Chair Programme, which was relaunched in 2013.

Now aged 94, Rams told Dezeen he sees FSB 1138 as an example of everyday design that is so distinctive it "speaks for itself".

"Such products are rare, but they serve as an essential source of inspiration and encouragement for the way we shape our environment," he explained. "They become a benchmark for the future."

Rams developed the door handle with support from his student Angelika Knoop and Petr Tučný in response to a brief that invited designers to reflect on the question: "Is it even possible to create new forms anymore?"

Among the other workshop participants were Hans-Ullrich Bitsch, Shoji Hayashi, Hans Hollein, Arata Isozaki and Alessandro Mendini. Of the nine concepts developed, the designs by Hollein, Mendini and Rams were added to FSB's product range.

Read:

Dieter Rams "regrets contributing to culture of overconsumption" says documentary director

The original RGS (Rams Grau Schwarz) version of the door handle was manufactured using aluminium and thermoplastic.

The aluminium component was produced at FSB's factory in Brakel, but the thermoplastic part had to be sourced externally. Due to its substandard performance in terms of longevity, the product was discontinued in 2005.

The new version features an all-metal aluminium construction, which will allow the handle to develop a unique patina over years of use.

The updated door handle retains the core design DNA of its predecessor, which, according to FSB's original 1980s brochure, set out to "create a simple yet highly visible statement amid the general chaos of formal diversity".

"The circle communicates the turning movement, while the recess and the softly curved handle naturally indicate the position of the hand, ensuring a secure, comfortable and effortless grip," explained Dr Klaus Klemp, author of Dieter Rams: The Complete Works.

"Its function is immediately understandable. It is a perfect example of beauty emerging from function."

Rams was involved throughout the development process and endorsed all of the updates to the product.

The 1986 workshop marked the beginning of FSB's international collaborations with architects and designers, with John Pawson, Heike Falkenberg, David Chipperfield and Foster + Partners among the more recent contributors to the firm's product catalogue.

Rams retired from Braun in 1997 but continues to advise Vitsoe, which also produces a re-engineered version of his 621 side tables. He is known to have influenced designers such as Jasper Morrison and former Apple chief design officer Jony Ive.

In a 2019 interview with Dezeen, Gary Hustwit, the director of a documentary film about Rams, said the designer regretted the part he played in driving a global culture of overconsumption.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: Berlin furniture brand Objekte Unserer Tage has released the Sander seating island, the flexible younger sibling of its marshmallowy sofa model, which was designed with a central backrest that can be used from both sides.

Objekte Unserer Tage (OUT) wanted to create an updated version of its Sander sofa – a low-slung, chubby model that the brand affectionately refers to as a mountain of marshmallows.

Billed as "the most relaxed sofa of all time", the ultra-soft Sander has now been transformed into a seating island in response to the steady trend for open floor plans in both residential and public settings.

The island features a similar, squidgy form as the sofa, but is differentiated by a central backrest that can be reclined against from both sides.

OUT wanted to create seating that offers "more than a piece of furniture against the wall" and allows for rooms to be considered from different perspectives.

The furniture is suitable for generous living or large retail spaces where interior designers are seeking pieces to interrupt the floor plan.

"The Sander seating island connects spaces, structures, and areas and brings people together," said the brand.

Like all of OUT's furniture pieces, the seating island is handmade in Germany and is available in local upholstery.

Alternatively, OUT accepts textile commissions from clients who would like their furniture upholstered in fabrics by major textile brands such as Kvadrat or Dedar, or bespoke materials from independent sellers.

"The Sander sofa is our most successful design," said OUT. "From the first touch to the final stitch!"

"Now, Sander can be used from both sides, transforming it into an open seating island in the middle of the room," added the brand. "It speaks to the way that many architects and interior designers are working today."

OUT was founded in 2015. Based in Berlin, the brand works exclusively with artisans across Germany, from seamstresses in the Swabian Alps to carpenters in Bavaria.

A system of curtains divides areas filled with collectible furniture within this compact office, which LA-based Public Art Company has designed for its own team.

Public Art Company's studio on Hyperion Avenue in Los Angeles provides the design agency a colourful environment in which to devise and curate large-scale artworks for campuses, developments and public spaces.

Founder Raffi Lehrer and his colleagues renovated the space and filled it with contemporary artworks and collectible furniture to create a bold, eclectic environment.

"A friend once called it 'muppets on acid'," said Lehrer, who set up the company in 2020.

Drop-ceiling panels were replaced with polycarbonate sheets to reveal the structure above, while cork tiles provide a soft, acoustically optimised floor.

A raised platform was added at the back of the space, and a curtain system by Carlos Medellin allows the room to be reconfigured for meetings, parties or open studio use as required.

These translucent drapes in white, blue, grey and orange are mounted on ceiling tracks that cut diagonally across the room, curve around corners and wrap its perimeter.

In the centre, a chunky blue table and chair set by Matt Nichols offers a space for casual meetings and conversation.

Read:

Charlap Hyman & Herrero adds custom workstations to futuristic LA office

A large humanoid sofa named Pepita the Couch and a small pink lamp, both by Katie Stout, occupy one side of the back platform along with a NeuroWeave carpet by Güvenç Özel.

Green chairs by Danish architect Bjarke Ingels for Fritz Hansen are positioned beside a window, which is adorned with text graphics by Ben Klevay.

More of Klevay's colourful, paper typographic signage works cover another wall, while sculptures by Misha Kahn further enliven the space.

Artworks by Julieta Gil, Kumkum Fernando and Philip Mueller also decorate the studio, along with furniture pieces including a desk and a green candelabra that Lehrer built himself.

The variety of design and creative agencies in Los Angeles means that the city is full of eclectic workspaces.

Charlap Hyman & Herrero recently added custom workstations to a futuristic office, West of West placed a sculptural wood staircase at the heart of Puma Studios and 22RE created a "distinctly Californian" workspace in the former studio of artist Ed Ruscha.

item.content:encoded:
Local studio Lenka Milerová Architektka has converted a former pigsty in the Czech Republic into Panoší Újezd Summer House, complementing its rough stone walls with additions in exposed concrete.

The holiday home, which is named after the nearby village, was created within the former pigsty for the owner of the adjacent home.

Despite the poor condition of the pigsty, the owner had a long, personal connection to the site that ruled out demolition and reconstruction.

Lenka Milerová Architektka took a "raw, industrial" approach to the transformation, celebrating the existing stone and brick structure and making new additions in concrete and steel.

"The architectural approach centred on exposing the structural materials and utilizing the most basic construction techniques," said founder Lenka Milerová.

"Concrete became the medium for detail," she continued. "The result is not ostentatious architecture. On the contrary. The roughness, imperfection, and simplicity connect with the atmosphere of the place and highlight what has been present here from the very beginning."

The pigsty's single room was opened up through the introduction of two steel-framed openings – a glass pivot door that creates an entrance from the garden, and a large, deep-set window that frames a view back towards the main house.

At the back of the site, a small bathroom was carved out of a slope in the terrain, and is separated from the living area by a sliding wooden door. Inside, this bathroom was finished with boardmarked concrete walls and is illuminated by a skylight and window.

A low concrete podium was added around the perimeter of the interior, creating space for a daybed beneath the living area's window and extending to support a bathtub in the bathroom.

While the existing stone walls were cleaned and left exposed, the sections of brick wall were treated with a textured cement spray, contrasting the smoothness of the new concrete additions.

Read:

Madeleine Architects converts pigsty into The Recipe house in Switzerland

"The intervention that transformed the space most dramatically was the creation of new window openings lined with monolithic concrete jambs," explained Milerová.

"This flows seamlessly into a concrete bench running around the perimeter of the main, and only, room. It serves as a step, storage space for wood, a sofa, and a bath," she added. "The roughness, imperfection, and simplicity connect with the atmosphere of the place and highlight what has been present here from the very beginning."

Aside from this concrete podium, the interior of the summer house has been left deliberately sparse and flexible, with the only other fixed element being a small concrete counter with a sink in one corner.

Alongside the building, a small outdoor kitchen has been created overlooking a patio, accessed via a paved path that leads around from the entrance.

Other pigsty conversions featured on Dezeen include a project by Madeleine Architects in Switzerland, for which the studio wrapped the existing structure in a layer of lime and hemp to create the base of a home and office.

Elsewhere in the Czech Republic, BekArch recently converted a disused bakery workshop into a skylight-topped apartment.

The photography is by Radek Šrettr Úlehla.
