Dezeen School Shows: a proposal for a waterside repair and reuse hub exploring craft, material reuse and environmental stewardship is among projects from the University of Plymouth.

Also featured is a regenerative laboratory restoring Plymouth Sound's seabed and a proposal to transform polluted harbour water into a resource for marine research, industry and public engagement.

University of Plymouth

Institution: University of Plymouth
School: School of Art, Design and Architecture
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture and Master of Architecture
Tutors: Alessandro Aurigi, Nikolina Bobic, Ricky Burke, Graham Devine, Mathew Emmett, Andy Humphreys and Sana Murrani

School statement:

"Architecture at the University of Plymouth is explored as a civic, environmental and material practice. The work asks how buildings, landscapes and institutions can support social and ecological life, and how design can shape futures responsive to the conditions of the present.

"Across undergraduate and postgraduate projects, students examine architecture as a way of connecting people, resources, knowledge and place.

"The projects showcased here focus on two settings of civic and environmental consequence in Plymouth: the working waterfront and the university campus.

"Postgraduate students worked through live engagement with Plymouth Fisheries and related stakeholders to reimagine the Fish Quay after the closure of the fish auction, asking how waterfront renewal might support the coexistence of small-scale fisheries, public access, marine ecology, local food economies and climate adaptation.

"Undergraduate students examined the university as a contested civic and knowledge institution through projects centred on the Students' Union, Campus Park and wider city connections.

"Throughout, architecture is framed as relationships between labour and ecology, institution and public life, material systems and long-term stewardship.

"Proposals for adaptive reuse, flexible adaptation and low-carbon material systems rethink how buildings are occupied, maintained and shared, supporting practices that can change over time."

Aperture Obscura: Mechanisms of Perception by Libby Volokh

"Aperture Obscura positions itself within Plymouth's reconstructed civic landscape as a mediator between everyday urban life and the distant realities of contemporary conflict and displacement.

"Located on Armada Way, a post-war axis shaped by wartime destruction and institutional reconstruction, the project explores how architecture can hold unresolved histories and present anxieties simultaneously.

"Through film, archive, and collective occupation, it seeks to recover voices obscured by conflict, drawing on the work of Martha Rosler, Paul Virilio and Gilles Deleuze.

"The adaptive reuse of the abandoned Salvation Army Congress Hall resists demolition, material extraction, replacement and civic erasure through reconstruction."

Student: Libby Volokh
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Mathew Emmett and Nikolina Bobic
Email: elizabethvolokh[at]gmail.com

Civic Assemblage by Ciaran Halpin

"What is the future role of the university? As institutions increasingly advocate lifelong learning, existing pedagogical frameworks struggle to support evolving relationships between education, industry and public life.

"Conventional models of teaching risk becoming isolated from the realities of material production and civic engagement.

"The Civic Assemblage emerges as an investigation into this condition, reimagining the university as an open, collaborative framework where making, learning and industry converge, thereby activating public participation and positioning education as a catalyst for social and urban transformation across Plymouth."

Student: Ciaran Halpin
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Ricky Burke and Alessandro Aurigi
Email: ciaran.halpin[at]outlook.com

Second Nature: Learning through Waste, Repair and Reuse by Holly Salmons

"This project addresses the UK's lack of education, responsibility and accountability around waste and recycling at both a national and domestic scale.

"Situated on the university's existing recycling centre, the project will localise the education and practice of upcycling and reuse.

"By involving students and the residents of Plymouth in practical lessons, and by making the sustainable, circular material processes that take place on site visible and integrated into public space, the project aims to change behaviours and attitudes towards over-consumption and carelessness regarding waste and recycling."

Student: Holly Salmons
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Andy Humphreys and Graham Devine
Email: hollsjs8[at]gmail.com

Pathologies of Place: Echoes of the Flesh by Freya Marchant

"Pathologies of Place retells narratives of bodies denied autonomy within Plymouth on both literal and socio-political levels.

"Examining the trajectory of the body, the project explores how certain bodies are pathologised and regulated through systems of care, control and spatial organisation, critiquing the influence of the Abercrombie Plan and scientific advancement in shaping perceptions of the body and space.

"The body is our basic means of having a world (Merleau-Ponty, 1945), yet it functions as a site of boundary-making (Butler, 1993), shaped by socio-political systems that tether it to normative and linear forms of being (Grosz, 1994).

"When disciplined and mechanised, the body is constrained by structures that enforce a predetermined trajectory (Betson, 2015).

"Can embodiment escape linearity in systems designed around a single privileged body? The project redistributes the body onto the building itself, producing moments of heightened proprioception.

"The building becomes responsive and metamorphic, adapting to Plymouth's landscape through Arduino-based reactive systems.

"The project forms an archive in which, by encountering forgotten narratives of Plymouth, the inhabitant is prompted to relearn what it means to inhabit a body within a post-human condition."

Student: Freya Marchant
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Nikolina Bobic and Mathew Emmett
Email: freyapebbles[at]outlook.com

The Generative Library by Oliver Mowbray

"The traditional library of social exchange has become a temple to the Cartesian human. This adaptation to the university library ruptures physical, socio-economic and socio-cultural barriers, exposing students to exchange and collaboration whilst preserving physical media.

"Reclaimed rubble in gabion baskets holds a historic resonance that patinas with ecologies, appropriation and adaptation.

"Architecture here is generated through occupation and living memory; non-human elements act as responsive participants, a pulsating reactor, expanding and contracting.

"Extended landings and crossings, whilst unmoving, allow a 'movement that is both integrative and exploratory' (Leatherbarrow, 2009, p. 224), inspiring serendipitous encounters and informal collaborative learning."

Student: Oliver Mowbray
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Ricky Burke and Alessandro Aurigi
Email: ojmowbray[at]outlook.com

Data for Democracy by Yola Troughton

"Data for Democracy aims to reclaim the power of digital data held by the opaque hands of a few, redistributing it democratically back into our own regional systems.

"By empowering and protecting our local civic infrastructure as we move into the new digital age, the scheme looks to a more socially and environmentally sustainable approach to data storage and handling, integrating citizens' assemblies and other civic workshops alongside a digital archive.

"Acting as an engine, the data centre powers discourse through access to contextualised information, while the excess thermal energy is harnessed through passive heating strategies to support the functions of the building."

Student: Yola Troughton
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Andy Humphreys and Graham Devine
Email: yola.troughton[at]gmail.com

Molecular Microplasti[cities]: Degradation as Disclosure by Charlie Hirst

"Molecular Microplasti[cities] addresses the growing threat of microplastic pollution in marine ecosystems.

"Located at Sutton Harbour, the project retrofits existing infrastructure to transform polluted harbour water into a resource for research, industry and public engagement.

"Water is purified through two filtration towers integrated into the architecture and then reused to support aquaculture, marine research and fish market operations.

"The towers also house modular living pods for researchers and fishing industry workers. By making the invisible visible — revealing the hidden presence of microplastics through architecture — the project becomes a monument to environmental change, promoting awareness, collaboration and sustainable marine regeneration."

Student: Charlie Hirst
Course: ARCH766 Design Praxis, Master of Architecture
Tutors: Mathew Emmett and Sana Murrani
Email: charlie_daniel[at]hotmail.co.uk

The Seabed Laboratory by Ben Howley

"The Seabed Laboratory responds to the long-term ecological decline of Plymouth Sound, where centuries of dredging and trawling have left soft scars across the seabed.

"The project treats these scars as opportunities for repair, positioning Fish Quay as a place where fishing communities and marine ecologists work together to restore the Sound.

"The old auction building is grafted onto new structures that support hatcheries, laboratories and seagrass workshops, while a recycled steel warehouse produces shellcrete reefs from waste scallop shells.

"A shellcrete tower shaped by kelp holdfasts marks the quay as a renewed landmark of restoration."

Student: Ben Howley
Course: ARCH766 Design Praxis, Master of Architecture
Tutors: Sana Murrani and Mathew Emmett
Email: benhowley3[at]gmail.com

[RE]Imagining Resilience Through System Thinking by Alastair Freeman

"Regenerative design extends beyond traditional sustainability by actively repairing ecosystems and enhancing the capacity of future generations to thrive.

"This proposal seeks to recycle waste from the fishing industry into seagrass pods that restore rare marine habitats in Plymouth Sound, an area where climate change poses significant threats to biodiversity.

"Repurposing this waste establishes a circular model that regenerates the marine food web while delivering enduring ecological and human benefits.

"Ultimately, the project aims to transform the built environment into resilient, productive habitats that support both natural ecosystems and human communities."

Student: Alastair Freeman
Course: ARCH766 Design Praxis, Master of Architecture
Tutors: Sana Murrani and Mathew Emmett
Email: freeman.alastair[at]gmail.com

In Mutual Dependence – Mending through material, craft and environment by Zi Jie Chan

"The project proposes a pavilion that rethinks construction through mutual dependence, where material, environment and users are interlinked rather than controlled.

"In Plymouth's maritime context of shipbuilding and repair, as well as Devon's regenerative woodland practices, it uses timber offcuts, reclaimed sail and rope to form a low-tech, reversible structure.

"Instead of resisting coastal forces such as salt, humidity and wind, the design embraces processes of weathering, mending and adaptation, allowing it to evolve over time.

"This project challenges conventional construction methods based on permanence and extraction, instead promoting circular, craft-based architecture grounded in material awareness, reuse and ongoing care."

Student: Zi Jie Chan
Course: ARCH763 Sustainable Technologies, Master of Architecture
Tutors: Andy Humphreys and Graham Devine
Email: zi.chan[at]postgrad.plymouth.ac.uk

item.content:encoded:
Continuing our Future Stadium series, we look at the revamp of the Estadio Santiago Bernabéu in Madrid, Spain, which shows how an existing stadium can be future-proofed.

Although numerous stadiums are built from the ground up every year, the reality is that many of the world's future stadiums already exist. Modern stadiums are some of the world's largest and most carbon-intensive buildings, and renovating them to extend their life is becoming increasingly important.

The extensive renovation of the Estadio Santiago Bernabéu, by GMP Architekten with L35 and Ribas & Ribas, demonstrates how an almost 80-year-old structure can be transformed to meet the 24/7 commercial needs of the world's biggest football club – Real Madrid.

"I think the big driver for the stadium's development is basically the full-time use," GMP Architekten director Martin Glass told Dezeen.

"You build an installation that is incredibly expensive, so you don't want to only use it for two hours a week, and in that context, of course, the question of flexibility becomes a major driver," he continued.

"So, the more things you can do – more bigger events, smaller events, events in parallel – and the more you can integrate a stadium within the community, the more you can make it something more than just a sports venue."

Originally opened in 1947, the stadium has since seen several ad-hoc renovations and expansions.

Costing over €1 bn, which Glass pointed out is "a lot of money for renovation", the latest revamp gave the stadium a complete overhaul, while maintaining the "identity, soul and character of the existing structure".

Along with elevating the experience of fans on match days, the renovation had two major goals – to enhance the brand of Real Madrid and improve the commercial potential of the building.

Visually, the most obvious aspect of the renovation is its new facade. GMP Architekten wrapped the original concrete structure entirely in stainless steel louvres to give the building, and the club, a new identity.

"The most striking feature of the renovation is, of course, the new facade and roof – these shiny bands of stainless steel that we wrapped around the stadium," said Glass.

"The original stadium had a concrete structure that was actually quite visible, but it was also a bit outdated and came from a time when stadiums were [thought] more as engineering tasks," he continued.

"We're living in this internet and Instagram world where the image becomes more and more important. Real Madrid are aware of this and wanted to create a visually striking image."

Although the stadium was entirely wrapped in this shiny facade, the overhaul of the money-generating capacity of the stadium represented a huge portion of the design effort.

This expansion was achieved through numerous additions that allow the building to be more widely used on non-match days. A retractable roof was added, a retractable pitch built, a new museum created, markets and food stands enhanced and a new panoramic viewpoint is planned for the heights of the structure.

Perhaps the most impressive of these additions is the Bernabéu's retractable pitch. Key components of a modern stadium, retractable pitches allow for the main arena to be regularly utilised without damaging the playing surface.

Most commonly, this involves creating a playing surface that can be lifted and rolled off the pitch – such as at Tottenham Stadium in London.

Read:

Ten stadiums of the future that rewrite the playbook

However, as the Estadio Santiago Bernabéu is surrounded by roads on all sides, this was not possible and instead the pitch is stacked in a giant, underground greenhouse.

"It's a very brave client that trusts technology, but it also comes from a necessity," said Glass. "Because of this super tight inner city situation, a solution like Tottenham, or Schalke here in Germany, where the retracted pitch just goes outside, which is of course way easier to build, is simply not possible."

"They have residential areas all around them and public streets, so there simply wasn't any possibility to do something other than stack it underground," he continued. "Also, the reason that they stack it on just one side is that on the other side, 50 metres underneath the pitch, they have a public metro line."

Along with the retractable pitch, the retractable roof allows the main arena to be quickly converted for use for concerts and other large-scale events.

Beyond the main arena, the architecture studios developed attractions for fans on non-match days that would go beyond the standard stadium tours, including a new museum, which was built on a bridge between two of the existing, concrete stair towers.

"The museum is actually a 150-metre-long bridge that is cantilevering above the ground because they were not allowed to build on public ground," said Glass.

"Only the Museo del Prado has more visitors [in Spain] than the Real Madrid Museum, and they are really expanding it a lot. The last time I was there, the prices were around 35 euros a visit, so it is absolutely a revenue generator."

The stadium also incorporates several restaurants, a brewery, Starbucks and the Bernabéu Market, which Real Madrid describes as a gastronomic district, all of which are open daily.

Following its renovation, the Santiago Bernabéu is set to host games at the upcoming World Cup in 2030, which takes place in Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. We recently rounded up all 23 stadiums that will host games at the tournament.

The photography is by Marcus Bredt.

Local architecture studio HYAN has renovated Green Sandwich House, a 1970s home in Japan, using a palette of timber, plaster and tiles to bring "warmth and texture" to a flexible, open living space.

Named after its setting enveloped by wooded hills in Hayama, south of Tokyo, Green Sandwich House was renovated for HYAN's founders, architect Anna Naganuma and designer Shohei Hasegawa.

Originally constructed in the late 1970s, the home required significant structural reinforcement to meet modern seismic codes, which the studio took as an opportunity to create airy, flexible interiors around the grid of the retained structural frame.

"The starting point was to inherit the house rather than demolish it. Preserving a 1970s house wasn't the goal in itself; we wanted to read the potential of the existing frame and update it for how we live today," Hasegawa told Dezeen.

"As both the designers and the residents, we don't see this as a finished work, but as a house that grows with our daily life," he added.

On the ground floor, almost all of the home's interior partitions were removed to create a single living, dining and kitchen space, with zoning created by changes in floor level and ceiling height.

The living area occupies a double-height space next to the kitchen and dining area, while alongside, the floor steps down slightly to create a lounge area with a nook for a daybed that can be closed off with patterned curtains.

This open layout, along with a simple material palette of pale plastered walls and timber floors, emphasises the presence of the reinforced timber columns and roof beams of the existing structure, which also suggest where the former partition walls once stood.

"Rather than dividing the kitchen, pantry, study and doma with walls, we connected them loosely as a single continuous space," explained Hasegawa.

"Work, daily life, hobbies and hosting friends all overlap naturally, while light, air and the surrounding scenery move through the whole house and give it a different character depending on the time of day and season," he added.

Read:

Kenta Hirayama clads House in Kinuta in steel-sheet facade

The interior surfaces are complemented by coloured tiles and terrazzo in the kitchen and bathroom, chosen in response to the play of light and shadow through the large windows and surrounding trees.

A staircase to one side of the ground floor space leads up to the more private first floor, which contains the home's bedrooms and a study overlooking the double-height living area.

"Wood, plaster and textiles - things with warmth and texture - kept alongside a restrained palette, so that the existing frame remains the protagonist," Hasegawa told Dezeen.

"More than being beautiful on their own, the materials matter for how they catch natural light and shadow and the changing seasons, tying the architecture, the landscape and daily life together," he added.

Elsewhere in Japan, the creation of a single, continuous living space was also central to House in Takahatayama by HYG Architects, and Kenta Hirayama clad a contemporary Tokyo home in steel sheets.

item.content:encoded:
The Atlassian Central skyscraper, designed by SHoP Architects and BVN Architecture, in Sydney, Australia, has become the world's tallest hybrid timber tower.

Designed as the Sydney headquarters for technology company Atlassian, the 180-metre-high office tower topped out earlier this week.

With a hybrid structure of timber, steel and concrete it overtakes the 86.6 -metre-high Ascent tower in Milwaukee, USA, by almost 100 metres, to become the world's tallest hybrid timber tower.

The 39-storey skyscraper has a unique hybrid structural system, with concrete cores supporting mass timber floors and internal structures, wrapped in a steel exoskeleton.

This exoskeleton supports seven "mega floors" that have been placed every four stories to divide the building vertically into what the design team described as "habitats".

These, primarily timber, habitats will contain office accommodation along with multi-floor atriums and elevated parks.

"SHoP has been privileged with the opportunity to design such an innovative project – one that we believe will redefine how people come together, collaborate, and create in Sydney and beyond," said SHoP Architects associate principal Andreia Teixeira.

"It's particularly rewarding to begin experiencing the spatial qualities of a high-rise that reimagines a natural habitat within an urban tower – connecting people to each other, nature and to the city around them," she continued.

"We're excited by how this concept sets a new benchmark for sustainability, where timber, landscape, and natural ventilation come together to shape a more holistic work-life experience and inspire future innovation."

According to the design team, the use of timber has reduced the overall building weight and carbon impact, while the steel and concrete ensures strength and stability.

The design expects the design to reduce the upfront embodied carbon by 50 per cent compared to a conventional steel and concrete office tower.

The team aims to also achieve a 50 per cent improvement in operational energy efficiency compared to a conventional 5 Star NABERS base building.

Read:

Studio Gang exposes mass-timber structure of Rubenstein Treehouse at Harvard

"Hybrid mass timber has done more than reduce embodied carbon, it has fundamentally shaped how tower buildings can be delivered, enabling prefabrication, dry construction and a faster, lighter vertical build," said BVN principal Peter Titmuss.

"As a prototype for mass-timber towers of the future, this is a moment of global significance."

The tower sits next to Sydney Central Station and was built over an existing historic building called The Parcels Shed that was once used for taking deliveries of parcels and then turned into a youth hostel.

SHoP Architects and BVN plan to incorporate the youth hostel building into the lower levels of the tower.

The project is set to complete by the end of this year with facade installation currently being completed.

New York-based SHoP Architects was founded in 1996.

The practice has completed a series of monumental tower designs including 111 W 57th Street on Billionaires Row in Manhattan and Brooklyn's first supertall skyscraper.

BVN is an Australian architecture firm that has offices in Sydney, Brisbane, London and New York.

It recently joined forces with Copenhagen studio 3XN on projects such as Sydney Fish Market and Quay Quarter Tower in Sydney, which was named Best Tall Building Worldwide by the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat in 2023.

The photography is by Toby Peet.

item.content:encoded:
The Glasgow School of Art has announced that it cannot afford to rebuild the iconic Mackintosh Building without external funding, following the second fire that tore through the building in 2018.

According to an announcement made by the school yesterday, it has insufficient funds to reinstate the 1910 building by Charles Rennie Mackintosh, and it now plans to remove scaffolding surrounding the building to stabilise and expose its burned-out shell.

However, it said it will look to secure external funding to help enable reinstating the Mackintosh Building in the future.

"The school cannot possibly, on its own, rebuild this whole building," according to its chair of the board of governors Ann Priest.

"It would take us away from financial sustainability," she told the BBC.

Restoration "beyond the capacity and expertise of the school"

The announcement follows the settlement of a long-running arbitration claim with the building insurers regarding the 2018 blaze. Details of what was awarded have not been disclosed, but the school said it had offered "financial clarity" about what was possible.

It now estimates the cost of a full reinstatement to be around £265 million, which is "equivalent to five times the GSA's annual turnover" and four times more than a previous £62 million estimate.

"The scale of such a project would be beyond the capacity and expertise of the school and, despite reaching a positive settlement with insurers, the funding gap is significant due in large part to the rising costs of construction projects," said the report.

Priest added the Glasgow School of Art (GSA) is now looking for "visionary individuals" who could bring "serious investment" to the project, reported the BBC.

Scaffolding to be removed to expose shell

Affectionately known as the Mack, the fire-torn art school was the best-known building designed by Mackintosh, Scotland's most famous architect.

The first fire ripped through the art school in 2014, before a second, more destructive fire occurred in 2018 during a £35 million restoration project.

With restoration works now on hold, the school plans to remove the scaffolding that wraps the building and stabilise its shell with a mix of temporary and permanent internal supports.

The report outlines several options for moving forward, including partial reinstatement of the building. It also suggests the potential for the anchor of a "creative and cultural production innovation district", including nearby cultural institutions.

GSA's announcement has come as bad news to many who recognise the building as an iconic landmark in Scotland. Among them is architect Alan Dunlop, who described the announcement as "opaque".

Announcement is "travesty of epic proportions"

"What disappoints me most is the statement from the chair of governors saying that the Mackintosh can "have a new purpose and become a catalyst for innovation, regeneration and economic growth for Glasgow'," he wrote on Instagram.

"This seems to me to be a dilution of responsibility, and worse, a distinct failure to focus on their prime task of delivering a replacement for the Mackintosh building, rather than some centre for creative activity. It's clear to me still that a trust has to be set up, separate from the board."

In another post, he added "it is now clear that Mackintosh’s masterwork is gone forever", and called for efforts to retain as much as what is left as possible.

"For that we need an exceptional architect and a proper procurement process, not one like before that emphasises fee over talent and which recognises that this is the most important commission in Scotland and probably the UK," he wrote.

Meanwhile, Historic England's heritage at risk projects officer Lisa Rigg said it was an "absolute travesty of epic proportions".

"Where is the 21st-century Carnegie? Or the high-net-worth individuals, some of whom own swathes of the Scottish Highlands, ready to step in and save this iconic and pioneering art school building in its hour of need?" she wrote on LinkedIn.

Read:

Investigation into Glasgow School of Art fire fails to find "definitive cause"

In a shared statement, the Royal Institute of British Architects and Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland called on the government to help with the rebuild.

"We need leadership from the Scottish and UK Governments to find the resources needed to ensure the faithful reinstatement of the Mackintosh Building, and to secure its future as a revitalised creative hub serving Glasgow, Scotland and the world," read the statement.

In 2022, an inquiry into the cause of the second fire at the building failed to conclude due to insufficient evidence.

However, the report revealed that fifty per cent of the building was alight within 38 minutes of the firefighters arriving at the site. It is believed that this "uncontrolled fire growth and rapid development" was exacerbated by the restoration works.

Shortly after the second blaze, the former director of the Glasgow School of Art Tom Inns said that it would be rebuilt.

"It is as vital a part of the Glasgow School of Art's future as it has been for the last 100 years," Inns told Dezeen at the time. "We will rebuild so that 'the Mack' can continue to provide creative inspiration to students, staff and visitors."

item.content:encoded:
Our cities are full of apartment blocks dotted with pathetically sized balconies too small to be of any actual use, writes Jessica Furseth.

If no one ever sits there, is a balcony still a balcony? I found myself pondering this question as I was walking the perimeter of the Isle of Dogs in East London, an area where new blocks of flats seem to pop up like mushrooms.

These river-facing balconies should have made a great place to sit on that lovely summer evening, but save for the occasional lone smoker, they appeared deserted. There's a simple explanation, of course: the balconies are just too small.

Developers know they can charge more for this ephemeral idea with only a tokenistic gesture towards it

You know the ones – they are absolutely everywhere in most major cities around the world. They're cut into the face of a housing block, or sometimes hanging off the wall, measuring little more than a metre deep and two across, often facing a loud and dusty road.

That's just enough space for you, during the initial property viewing, to step outside and exclaim, "Oh there's a balcony!" This is the best moment you'll ever have out on that thing, because it's too poky to be of any real use.

They fit a drying rack, maybe a bicycle (my ex had a bike stolen off his balcony three floors up, which was frankly impressive). You can just about squeeze in that dinky table and chair set from IKEA, the Tärnö that's advertised as "a perfect size for the balcony".

Read:

Ten buildings that make a sculptural feature of their balconies

But this isn't Paris, where people survey the cityscape below over croissants and coffee – this is Hackney, where balconies with dirty railings are choking in the road dust from Mare Street, empty in the gorgeous sunset.

And yet, we continue to build them. The pandemic really impressed upon us the benefit of private outdoor space, as a place to enjoy fresh air without risk. It's not about the virus anymore, but perhaps some fear of the commons lingers.

Size notwithstanding, balconies do carry a lot of outdoor feelings – there's a sense of breathing space, and outdoor seclusion is a little exciting. Developers and estate agents know they can charge more for this ephemeral idea with only a tokenistic gesture towards it, whose practical uselessness is only revealed once we've moved in. By then, the money has already changed hands.

Even Juliet on her namesake balcony was close enough to speak to Romeo

Long before the pandemic pressed the issue of separate balconies, the idea was a feature in evolved societies: people should have decent housing, and if they can't have a garden they should at least have a veranda.

But while a concrete box on the 20th floor will provide air, it gives people none of the social functions of the garden. Even Juliet on her namesake balcony was close enough to speak to Romeo.

"At 100 feet, the balcony loses all social connection with the ground," writes Alistair Cartwright, an architectural historian at the University of Liverpool. "One cannot imagine calling up for a lapel pin and a loaf of bread to one of these postwar balconies, as the destitute poet Albert Llanas is said to have done to an old acquaintance in 1920s Barcelona."

Read:

Bright yellow balconies enliven Melbourne apartment block by Austin Maynard Architects

Today, urban conversations about terraces are primarily about light and air, not connection to our neighbours and communities. National standards leave the details to local policies, but according to the London Housing Design Guide from the mayor of London, "private outside space is desirable in all circumstances". The total size depends on the number of occupants, but a balcony should always be at least 1.5 metres deep.

The guide does say that this space can be added to the inside of the house in exceptional circumstances. I would have loved that when I lived in Haggerston, east London, where I had a balcony I'm pretty sure was slimmer than regulation.

It faced a narrow courtyard like in the Alfred Hitchcock film Rear Window, and the sensation of surveillance was a strong deterrent from enjoyment. Adding insult to injury, that terrace also cut into my miniscule living room, and I would have far preferred to have that space inside instead.

Another option is to trade private outdoor space for more public amenities

In New York, the balconies are even tinier than in London – a report by Curbed found several examples at just 45 centimetres width, and not even IKEA can help you with that. Architect and zoning expert Walter Marin grew philosophical when asked by Curbed to comment on this level of stinginess, speculating that New York balconies may not actually be about spending time out there, but more like a cold plunge. The point is to step outside for a moment and take a deep breath, before heading back inside.

Even as people admit to getting little use out of their diminutive balconies, I've found my suggestion to get rid of them altogether a hard sell. ("It's not great, but it's fine," my boyfriend Tom said about his ridiculous terrace, a trifle defensively.)

But there are alternatives. On a recent train journey out of Waterloo station I noticed how balconies facing the rail tracks were enclosed to protect them from noise and dust. Part of the new developments in Nine Elms, south London, these glazed, ventilated winter gardens are a way to enjoy such space year-round, wasting nothing.

Read:

"An architectural style has emerged that I'm calling 'gentleism'"

Other countries are also building these enclosed terraces. A walk past new waterfront developments in Tallinn, Estonia, for example, will showcase dozens of buildings with balconies featuring a glass pane that can be opened or closed depending on the weather. A tiny balcony thus becomes a light-filled bonus room in winter, when the temperature can stay below freezing for months at a time.

Another option is to trade private outdoor space for more public amenities. Maybe you don't get your own balcony, but there's a roof garden, or a new park nearby. In south London, Lambeth Council requires new developments to have at least 50 square metres of shared amenity space, in addition to 10 square metres of private balcony space per flat.

Many London councils have similar rules to Lambeth where, if amenity space can't be provided on-site, the money can go to an off-site provision. The challenge, as ever, is ensuring that what gets delivered is of sufficient quality – there are also far too many bleak, concreted plazas permanently in the shade.

It might be better to put that square footage back inside homes where it can be of use

I gave up on tiny balconies for good after my Hitchcock situation in Haggerston. These days I prefer going to the park – even though I share it with innumerable dogs and runners (both off-leash and equally prone to bumping into you), I far prefer the greenery and feeling of open space.

Private terraces for all is a nice idea, but it doesn't seem to be working for people; we're just not using our tiny balconies. Yes, we need outdoor space, but they aren't meeting our needs.

It might be better to put that square footage back inside homes where it can be of use, and turn our focus towards making better communal outdoor space. If given a choice between a useless balcony where I'm alone with my drying rack, or a green garden shared with my neighbours, I know what I'd choose.

Jessica Furseth is a journalist based in London. Her writing has appeared in The Guardian, Vox, Time Out, Huck, The Cut, Atlas Obscura, Vice, The Independent, and elsewhere.

item.content:encoded:
Design studios Softlab and Moment Factory have created seven immersive installations for the 350-metre-high Edge NYC skyscraper viewpoint at Hudson Yards, including a massive kaleidoscope and a series of pulsating globes.

Edge NYC, which is the highest indoor-outdoor sky deck in the Western Hemisphere, is set on the 100th floor of Kohn Pedersen Fox's 30 Hudson Yards skyscraper.

The recently opened, immersive installations are intended to create an additional experience to its bird's-eye view of Manhattan. Similar to ones designed by art collective TeamLab, the artworks were created to be walked through and experienced in person.

Among the first installations in the visitor route is Pulse, which was designed by Softlab and features 450 pulsating globes across a number of rooms that shift in colour as visitors walk past them.

"Pulse is really about capturing the energy of New York City," Softlab director Michael Szivos told Dezeen.

"The 450 globes represent the city as a world within worlds, while the shifting gradients and interactive choreography reflect how individual actions contribute to the collective energy of the city."

The studio hoped that the installation would evoke "a sense of curiosity" and aimed for it to change with each visit.

"The colour palette is derived from Edge's brand colours, which are inspired by the changing colours of the sky throughout the day – from midday to sunset and twilight," Szivos said.

"We organised these into warm and cool gradients that continuously shift and transition, allowing the installation to move between contrasting atmospheres through generative behaviours, so the experience is never exactly the same twice."

Also among the installations is Kaleidoscope, a series of rooms that includes a main artwork that Edge NYC says is "New York's largest kaleidoscope" and was designed by Moment Factory.

"The goal was to design an interior experience that acts as a mirror to the city's dynamic nature," Moment Factory creative director Patrick Bisson told Dezeen.

"By treating the space as a prism that refracts New York's radiant energy, we provide a distinct sensory engagement that complements the outdoor sky deck before visitors even step outside."

The largest kaleidoscope lets visitors step inside it to be surrounded by shifting, colourful prisms in changing patterns.

"The installation was designed to function as a multifaceted prismatic space, integrating digital media with highly reflective architectural surfaces," Bisson said.

"This approach captures the physical movement of the visitors, blending their reflections directly into the content," he continued.

"The result is a complex matrix of shifting geometry and light, creating a multiplicity of reflections that ensures an infinite, constantly evolving spatial experience."

Read:

New York's art deco icons inform revamped restaurant at The Edge

As well as the main kaleidoscope, Moment Factory also created numerous smaller kaleidoscopes, including one featuring street photography of New York City.

"The smaller kaleidoscope is designed as an intimate moment for guests to connect directly with the fabric of the city," Bisson said.

"We curated a street photography aesthetic that highlights urban textures and architectural geometry, interspersed with iconic landmarks."

The immersive installations also include Reflections, a kinetic sculpture made from 200 mirrored surfaces, and Crystal Cave, a 25-foot canopy of giant crystals, among others.

While most of the installations are located on the same floor as the Edge NYC viewpoint itself, there is also Skyrise, a "cinematic elevator experience" and Prism, an entryway experience that shows shifting views of New York.

The overall designs were all inspired by Edge itself, according to experience agency Journey, which oversaw the strategy for the project.

"We examined what already made Edge NYC so distinctive: its angular and triangular architecture, its use of glass and light, and its powerful vantage point to offer visitors new perspectives of New York City – both physically and mentally," said Journey strategy and creative lead Olivia Reid.

"From this foundation – and the visual language of triangles and prismatic energy – the strategic process enabled us to set and safeguard the experiential vision."

The Edge also features the newly revamped restaurant Peak designed by Journey, while other Hudson Yards attractions include Heatherwick Studio's Vessel and The Shed venue, which features a telescoping roof.
